title: Vomiting while on long-term prednisolone — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

blocks.text: Vomiting while on long-term prednisolone — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

Round 5 • PACES Station 2: acute consultation • Skills C communication, E clinical judgement, F managing concerns, G welfare (with focused A/B/D where relevant) • 20 minutes • Educational examiner-style encounter • Prepared 14 October 2026 • Not an official PACES mark scheme

You are the medical registrar in the emergency assessment unit. A 58-year-old with inflammatory disease has taken prednisolone for months but has vomited repeatedly and missed tablets for 2 days. They feel faint. Assess and explain your plan.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected adrenal crisis from glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency, precipitated by illness and missed steroids. Trap: Suspected adrenal crisis is an emergency: do not rely on oral prednisolone during persistent vomiting or delay parenteral hydrocortisone for blood results.

rows: “First I need to check if this is affecting your immediate safety.”
“I have a working diagnosis but need to exclude dangerous alternatives.”
Sepsis, hypovolaemic shock and other causes may coexist and must be investigated; do not make treatment wait for cortisol testing.
I am concerned your body may not have enough steroid while you are unwell. We will give hydrocortisone by injection and fluids immediately.

ABCDE, call senior/critical-care support, immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone, IV 0.9% saline and glucose correction as needed; monitor haemodynamics, electrolytes and glucose; look for infection/trigger.
After recovery I will arrange endocrine follow-up, sick-day rules, an NHS Steroid Emergency Card and injection-kit education if indicated.
Check patient priorities, understanding and follow-up.

blocks.text: Opening line: “I could not keep my steroids down. I am dizzy when I sit up. Should I try another tablet?” The actor is concerned but able to engage unless the examiner introduces deterioration. Release only history in the candidate brief; do not volunteer a diagnostic label. Ask “Why do you need to do that?” after proposed treatment. Acknowledge clear, compassionate explanations.

Q1. Why is this patient unstable?
Model answer: BP 84/52, HR 116 and low glucose during vomiting in a long-term steroid user point to shock and possible adrenal crisis.

Q2. Do you need a cortisol measurement first?
Model answer: No. If feasible take a sample first without delay, but hydrocortisone and resuscitation take priority.

Q3. What immediate steroid treatment?
Model answer: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately; then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg every six hours IV/IM.

Q4. What else needs treatment?
Model answer: Monitor and treat hypoglycaemia, give 0.9% saline with reassessment, and investigate and treat infection or other triggers.

Q5. What prevents recurrence?
Model answer: Endocrine review, written sick-day guidance, steroid emergency card and training for emergency injection if indicated.
Curveball: The patient deteriorates. Stop the routine consultation; summon emergency help and repeat ABCDE with immediate treatment.

FAIL — “Try more oral prednisolone and wait for the cortisol result.” The candidate ignores shock and inability to retain tablets.

PASS — “Your blood pressure is dangerously low, and vomiting means you may not be absorbing your steroid. I am calling for urgent help and giving injected hydrocortisone and fluids now.” The candidate monitors glucose, electrolytes and response.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — “We will treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately while also checking for infection and other causes of collapse. We will repeat your blood pressure, glucose and salts, and arrange an endocrine prevention plan once you are safe.”
